title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: France attributes the October refrigeration sabotage to Iran’s IRGC, citing at least 15 fires and disruption at small hydroelectric plants
items.content_text: On 9 November France’s cyber crisis centre, including ANSSI, formally attributed the 11–12 October sabotage of refrigeration controllers at about 700 French stores to Shahid Kaveh, a unit of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard that US agencies earlier linked to CyberAv3ngers. ANSSI says raised defrost settings caused food losses and at least 15 fires, and it also cites moderate disruption at small hydroelectric sites running Schneider Electric equipment. Evidence includes shared tooling, infrastructure and Persian-language traces; Paris prosecutors seek arrest warrants, France summoned Iran’s ambassador and will press for EU sanctions; on 10 November Iran’s Foreign Ministry rejected the accusation as groundless. This is a government attribution, not a court finding, and it does not cover the separate early-November wave across about 11 countries. Treat any internet-reachable controller, in any sector, as a target of a state-backed actor.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: The Record (9 Nov 2026, French report and Foreign Minister statement); SecurityWeek (10 Nov 2026, ambassador summoned); Anadolu Agency (10 Nov 2026, Iranian denial); Tech Times, citing Reuters (10 Nov 2026, ANSSI indicators and fires); CERT-FR; The Hacker News (9 Nov 2026, CISA/FBI joint warning)
_otthreatfeed.date_note: French attribution 9 Nov 2026; attack 11–12 Oct 2026; judicial investigation and EU sanctions effort ongoing

items.title: CISA and FBI warn of an ongoing threat to internet-connected refrigeration as European supermarket attacks reach at least 11 countries
items.content_text: Hackers are tampering with internet-connected refrigeration controllers in European supermarkets, and on 5 November CISA and the FBI, with HHS, USDA and DOT, warned the threat is ongoing and also reaches healthcare, chemical, transport and cold-storage operations. Hundreds of French stores were hit in October; a second wave on 1–2 November reached about 11 countries, forcing units into continuous heating or defrost, and three French blood-service sites had settings changed with no blood lost. No actor is named for this second wave, and a pro-Russian claim is unverified; on 9 November France attributed the separate 12 October attack to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard (see top story). Exposure is falling but not gone: exposed Danfoss StoreView instances dropped from 3,004 to 708 between 9 October and 5 November (The Hacker News, 9 November). If a controller is reachable from the internet, treat it as at risk today.

items.title: PHP2Shell attacks rooted about two dozen Palo Alto firewalls, and Siemens, Schneider and ABB now list grid-control, DCS and RTU products, several with no fix
items.content_text: Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified on 29 October that a suspected China-nexus actor chained the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) with Linux kernel bug CVE-2026-46300 to gain root on about two dozen internet-exposed PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October, then stole Active Directory credentials. Victims were in the US, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea. The OT exposure widened: Siemens now lists Spectrum Power grid-control systems and AMIS TS, Schneider lists a Foxboro DCS server, and ABB lists Netcontrol RTUs and ASPECT gateways, several with no fix yet. Attribution is suspected, not confirmed, and no Siemens, Schneider or ABB product is reported exploited. No OT operator has been named, so treat this as an IT-to-OT boundary warning.

items.title: The Pentagon is treating August freezer failures at US military base stores as a suspected cyberattack, Reuters reports
items.content_text: Reuters reported on 29 October, citing four unnamed officials, that investigators are treating late-August refrigeration failures at no fewer than six US military commissaries, including Fort Huachuca and Fort Irwin, as a suspected cyberattack: refrigerators and freezers switched to defrost mode and warmed, spoiling food. Army and Air Force investigators, including an Army cybercrime unit, opened inquiries soon after, US Cyber Command has since joined, and one official said investigators have spoken with French police about the October supermarket attack. The Pentagon says it is working closely with interagency and law-enforcement partners and has not confirmed a cause. Reuters could not establish whether the stores used Danfoss equipment, though records for the commissary at Naval Air Facility El Centro list a Danfoss control system. Nextgov/FCW, citing two unnamed sources, reports officials suspect Iran-linked hackers; no agency has attributed it. The entry route and any responsible party are not established.

items.title: SANS survey: a third of industrial organizations reported a cyber incident this year, and most of those incidents disrupted operations
items.content_text: The SANS Institute’s 2026 State of ICS/OT Security survey, released on 10 November, found that 34% of nearly 700 industrial respondents had a cyber incident, up from 22% last year and the largest one-year jump in the survey’s history; 72% of those incidents disrupted operations. Shared IT/OT credentials and ransomware tied as the most common incident types (31% each), and incidents affecting safety rose from 8% to 13%. Resilience is thin: only 15% could run critical operations manually for more than 48 hours, 40% do not know, and 58% say they would be unable to operate within a year if their main automation vendor disappeared. These are self-reported survey results, not incident data.

items.title: Check Point links three China-nexus spying campaigns to one malware supplier, with telecoms and critical-infrastructure operators among the targets
items.content_text: Check Point Research said on 10 November that a tool developer it calls CopperDragon supplies the Sparrow malware family to several China-nexus groups, including FamousSparrow, Earth Estries and Tropic Trooper, and it ties three campaigns together through that toolset. One, OceanGate, starts on internet-facing Linux servers and moves into Windows networks over RDP using new backdoors and kernel-level techniques; another uses watering-hole sites, some in shipping, that push fake “certificate fix” utilities. Targets span telecoms, government, military, research and critical infrastructure across Asia, Europe and Latin America. No OT intrusion or disruption is described and no CVE is named; for OT defenders the lesson is the entry path, exposed Linux servers and RDP, which also lead toward plant networks.

items.title: A jailbroken AI agent ran a two-week intrusion into a European telecom and its hosted customers, starting from a Cisco BroadWorks flaw now in KEV
items.content_text: Malbear Labs said on 8 November that it found an attacker’s exposed working directory holding more than 70 session transcripts, showing an agent built on a jailbroken DeepSeek model carrying out most of an intrusion into a European telecommunications provider and 13 organizations hosted on its infrastructure. The agent got in through CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated flaw in Cisco BroadWorks fixed in August, then used years-old Liferay and JBoss bugs to gain root and a second foothold, switching approach on its own when blocked. Its reports claim credentials, billing and patient records and Zabbix monitoring backups, none of it independently verified. CISA added the BroadWorks flaw to KEV on 10 November. Malbear judges the operator likely Chinese but names no state link. For OT teams the lesson is speed: old, unpatched web apps and monitoring servers can be found and chained without a skilled human at the keyboard.

items.title: Volt Typhoon has used a rotating “Silent Train” relay network since 2023 to break into management platforms, with water, energy and transport among the victims, Lumen reports
items.content_text: Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs reported on 28 October that Volt Typhoon has used “Silent Train”, a covert network of rapidly rotating, single-use chains of compromised small-office routers, IoT and enterprise devices, since November 2023 to reach targets and keep access to management and control-plane systems. Lumen ties the group to four confirmed zero-day campaigns and one likely one: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127, CVSS v3.1 10.0, Cisco), VeloCloud Orchestrator (CVE-2026-16812), N-able N-central (CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876), Versa Director (no CVE given) and, with moderate confidence, Quest KACE (no CVE). These are older flaws, not the VeloCloud flaw CVE-2026-114625 that CISA added to KEV on 23 October. Victims include telecoms, government, defence contractors, IT firms and MSPs, and universities, and Lumen lists water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation and emergency services among the critical-infrastructure sectors hit; Hawaii, California and Texas recur as focal points (Zero Day). No victim is named and no OT or ICS intrusion is described. Lumen points defenders to CISA’s Volt Typhoon guidance (AA24-038A) and its advisory on China-nexus covert networks (AA26-113A). Management and orchestration platforms often hold trusted paths into plant networks, which makes them the asset to protect here (editorial assessment).

items.title: Zyxel GS1900 managed switches: a new zero-day slipped past June’s fix, after attackers had already pulled data from about 1,000 of them
items.content_text: Binarly says CVE-2026-107441, an out-of-bounds write in the web-request handler of Zyxel’s GS1900 switches, gives root command execution to anyone who can reach the management interface without logging in, and that attackers already had a working exploit when it reported the bug on 29 September. Zyxel scores it 8.8 (Binarly 9.8). The June firmware that fixed the earlier GS1900 flaw, CVE-2026-7273 (in CISA KEV since 21 September), does not stop it; firmware 2.90 Patch 3, released 23 October, covers 10 models. GreyNoise linked theft of configuration data from 996 GS1900 switches around 17 August to the earlier flaw, and 564 of them still used factory passwords. Acronis ties the activity to a Chinese-speaking group it calls Red Heron, reported to deploy a backdoor and rootkit. Small managed switches like these are common in plant-floor and substation cabinets (editorial assessment).

items.title: OpenSSH “SSHole” lets an over-long password open password-less accounts on musl-based Linux; exploited within hours and now in KEV
items.content_text: OpenSSH 10.6p2 fixes CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS 8.1). On Linux builds that use the musl C library with PAM turned off, a password of 257 to 1,024 characters is accepted for accounts that have no usable password, including root on default Alpine setups. Previdian saw the first attempt less than nine hours after disclosure on 6 November and confirmed root on an Alpine honeypot; by 8 November it counted 20 attempts from 13 addresses, and watchTowr says only botnets and crypto miners have used it so far. CISA has added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Glibc-based distributions, Dropbear and systems that check passwords through PAM are not affected. musl-based embedded builds such as Buildroot, OpenWrt and Yocto sit inside many industrial gateways, routers and appliances, but no OT vendor has yet published an advisory, so whether a given product is exposed depends on how it was built (editorial assessment).

items.title: Barracuda gateway flaws that chain to root are now exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days to fix them
items.content_text: Barracuda disclosed two flaws on 4 November. CVE-2026-116606 (CVSS 9.3) lets an attacker who can reach the Email Security Gateway’s admin interface restore a crafted configuration backup without valid credentials; CVE-2026-111560 (CVSS 8.6), a command-injection bug that also affects Barracuda’s Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, WAF, WAF Control Center and Web Security Gateway, then runs commands as root. On 10 November CISA added both to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog with a 13 November deadline for federal agencies, and SecurityOnline reports that Barracuda has confirmed attacks on a small number of organizations and that exploit code is public. Email and web gateways are not OT, but at many utilities and plants they sit on the same corporate edge attackers use to reach domain credentials and remote-access paths into operations.

items.title: ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens finds the exploited Node2Shell bug in SIMATIC SCADA and PCS 7, and more OT vendors confirm PHP2Shell exposure
items.content_text: Siemens published nine advisories on 11 November covering ten flaws, two of them describing how the exploited Node2Shell (Brotli) bug reaches its products. High-severity issues touch SIMATIC SCADA and PCS 7, SIMATIC WinCC Graphics Designer, meta-iot2050, ROS#, Simcenter Femap and the Mendix Studio Pro MCP server, and could allow code injection or system compromise. Several products have no fix yet and some versions will not be fixed, so Siemens points customers to mitigations; it has seen Node2Shell exploitation attempts but no attacks aimed at its products. Schneider Electric fixed a medium-severity file-handling flaw in EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody, Johnson Controls fixed EasyIO Neo IO Manager and a C•CURE 9000/victor installer that could expose admin credentials, and Hitachi Energy and Phoenix Contact confirmed PHP2Shell impact. A day earlier CERT@VDE flagged a dozen bugs in Helmholz’s myREX24V2 remote-access server (fix 2.21.0) and Axis rated a Camera Station flaw 9.9 (CVE-2026-13312).

items.title: Siemens IoT2050 Node-RED flaw is now being exploited to plant botnet code and command backdoors
items.content_text: VulnCheck reports exploitation attempts against CVE-2026-58115, a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in the Node-RED web interface on SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced gateways running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed. Siemens published the advisory (SSA-834709) on 11 August. An unauthenticated remote attacker can create malicious flows and run code with full privileges. Observed attempts, seen on VulnCheck’s honeypots through 30 October, first downloaded a Linux botnet binary, then used a two-stage loader, and some requests instead created an HTTP endpoint that lets the attacker run commands and survives a reboot. The fix is Node-RED 4.3.4.1 or later; Siemens says to uninstall Node-RED or harden it if you cannot update. Honeypot hits show internet scanning, not confirmed compromise of any plant. A follow-up report on 8 November says Siemens widened the advisory on 4 November to further SIMATIC IoT2050 models when the affected Industrial OS and Node-RED versions are installed (Industrial OS V4.3.4-1 or later is the recommended fix); check the advisory for the current product list.

items.title: A researcher dumped 33 N-central zero-days with exploit code, forcing N-able to pull its hosted platform offline and rush out a hotfix
items.content_text: On 9 November a researcher published “Able2Shell”, 33 alleged flaws in N-able’s N-central remote monitoring and management platform with proof-of-concept code for each, including an unauthenticated XML chain that runs commands on the server and two chains that reach root. N-able took its hosted N-central environment offline, told on-premises customers to disconnect their servers, and on 10 November released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2, which fixes seven CVEs including CVE-2026-125883 (XXE) and CVE-2026-125881 (SSRF), both CVSS v4 9.3; a further hotfix is planned. Hosted servers have been upgraded. N-able reports scanning tied to the published code but no confirmed customer compromise, and watchTowr and Previdian saw attempts against honeypots. Volt Typhoon has exploited earlier N-central flaws (see Threat Intelligence & Research), and many integrators and MSPs use RMM tools to manage plant-side Windows hosts.

items.title: CISA adds an exploited SonicWall SSL VPN authentication bypass to its KEV catalog
items.content_text: On 6 November CISA added CVE-2026-19868 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. On SonicWall SSL VPN deployments with SAML sign-in enabled, a person holding valid credentials for a different authentication method can get past the intended check. SonicWall lists fixed firmware for Gen7 and Gen8 and offers no workaround. The sources do not say who is exploiting it or against whom. SSL VPNs are a common path for staff and integrators into plant networks, so the practical risk is an attacker arriving through the same door your remote-access users use.

items.title: Comments close 30 November on NIST’s draft rewrite of its OT security guide, which adds water, food, rail, maritime and building-automation coverage
items.content_text: NIST’s draft Revision 4 of SP 800-82, the US government’s main guide to operational technology security, is open for public comment until 30 November 2026. The draft reorganises the guide around Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, with risk management now led by the Govern function, and adds sector material for building automation, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and industrial IoT connected to cloud services. It also expands guidance on asset management, network monitoring and detection, protecting system-management functions, and applying zero-trust principles. Many regulators, insurers and auditors use 800-82 as a reference, so its final wording can shape what operators are asked to show; the comment window is the chance for practitioners to flag guidance that would not work on a plant floor.

items.title: Industry groups urge Congress to renew the 2015 cyber information-sharing law before its stopgap extension ends on 11 December
items.content_text: On 1 November a coalition of 35 industry groups, including water, public power, airline and business associations, wrote to the leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services committees asking them to keep a House defense-bill provision that would extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through 2035. The law gives legal protections to companies that voluntarily share cyber threat information with the government and each other, and its current temporary extension expires on 11 December 2026. The House defense bill carries the extension; as of Nextgov’s 2 November report no Senate extension had been agreed. For operators, the practical question is whether sharing through ISACs and with CISA keeps its current legal footing after that date.

items.title: EU cyber agency chief warns that after supermarket fridges, routers and home appliances could be next, and that AI is shrinking the time to exploitation
items.content_text: On 10 November ENISA’s executive director, Juhan Lepassaar, told AFP that security cannot be an afterthought, pointing to the refrigeration attacks that hit supermarkets in at least 12 European countries in October and November and warning that routers and home appliances could follow. An ENISA report released with his remarks calls AI a force multiplier for attackers and defenders and says the time between discovering a flaw and weaponising it is approaching zero. Its 2025 data show most incidents were ideologically driven, mostly low-impact denial-of-service by hacktivists, while ransomware did the most damage to businesses. ENISA also notes NIS2 is still not law in every member state, and the Cyber Resilience Act applies fully from December 2027.
